author: WeCult Editorial
original_title: This forgotten Rainbow Six spinoff would have thrived in a post-ARC Raiders world
summary_en: Released when battle royales were king, Rainbow Six Extraction tried a different path, a PvE extraction shooter that launched just before the genre exploded. Its unique blend of familiar operators and alien threats missed the mark for many, leading to its early demise.
ai_analysis: Extraction's PvE focus and unique take on the extraction loop highlight a missed opportunity to innovate in a genre that would soon become dominated by PvPvE experiences.

en.title: Rainbow Six Extraction: The Spinoff That Foresaw Gaming's Next Big Trend
en.summary: Released when battle royales were king, Rainbow Six Extraction tried a different path, a PvE extraction shooter that launched just before the genre exploded. Its unique blend of familiar operators and alien threats missed the mark for many, leading to its early demise.
en.body:
The early 2020s were a strange time for video games. The battle royale craze, ignited by **Apex Legends** in 2019, was starting to show signs of fatigue, leaving developers searching for the next big thing. In this uncertain landscape, **Ubisoft** released **Rainbow Six Extraction**, a PvE-focused spinoff that pitted the tactical operatives of Rainbow Six against a parasitic alien threat known as Archaeans. It was a bold, if somewhat ill-timed, experiment that drew heavily from the core mechanics of **Rainbow Six Siege**.

At its heart, **Extraction** offered a solid foundation with its familiar operators, each possessing unique abilities, and the tight gunplay fans expected. However, the game struggled to find its footing. Instead of the high-stakes scavenging and rapid exfiltration found in titles like **Escape from Tarkov**, **Extraction** leaned into a more structured PvE experience. Players were tasked with completing objectives within alien-infested zones, extracting with their squad, and managing their operators, who could become 'MIA' if they failed, requiring a rescue mission. While this offered a fresh take on the **Rainbow Six** formula, it lacked the depth and compelling loop that truly defines the extraction shooter genre, making it feel more like a Left 4 Dead-style cooperative shooter with a **Rainbow Six** skin.

## A Genre Ahead of Its Time?

**Ubisoft** ceased active development on **Rainbow Six Extraction** just a year after its release, a decision that might seem premature in hindsight. The game launched at a peculiar crossroads, before the explosion of PvPvE content and extraction-style games that would soon flood the market. Had it arrived even a year later, **Extraction** might have found a more receptive audience, potentially thriving in a world where games like **Hunt: Showdown** and **The Cycle: Frontier** were gaining traction, and even mainstream titles were experimenting with extraction mechanics. The developers were treading in largely uncharted territory, attempting to define a new subgenre with **Rainbow Six** operators and alien bioweapons, a combination that, while interesting, ultimately felt like a painter trying to depict a tiger without ever having seen one.

## What This Meant for Players

For the **Rainbow Six** community, **Extraction** represented a significant departure. While many appreciated the familiar operators and the core tactical shooting, the shift away from PvP and the unique extraction loop left some wanting more. The game was a gamble for **Ubisoft**, attempting to carve out a niche in a rapidly evolving market. It provided a fun cooperative experience for those looking to team up with friends and tackle challenging PvE content, but it failed to capture the magic that made **Siege** a global phenomenon, and it certainly didn't become the next big extraction shooter.

## What's Next

With **Ubisoft** having officially moved on from **Rainbow Six Extraction**, the future of the franchise remains focused on its flagship tactical shooter, **Rainbow Six Siege**, which continues to receive regular updates and support. No further content is planned for **Extraction**.

content_raw: The early 2020s were a liminal space in gaming, and not just because COVID wreaked havoc on our collective lives. Apex Legends was the defiant last stand of battle royales, debuting in 2019 before the genre fatigue hit with full force and no one knew exactly what was next. From that weird, feverish limbo arose Rainbow Six Extraction , a forlorn spinoff pitting the Rainbow operatives against zombified bioweapons called Archaeans. At its core, Extraction has a solid structure thanks to the gunplay and operators from Rainbow Six Siege , but lacks depth. Ela and Vigil are among the familiar faces in Rainbow Six Extraction . Image via Ubisoft The potpourri of Rainbow Six and a Left 4 Dead wannabe makes for a fun way to kill time, but it’s hardly Game of the Year material. Ubisoft ceased development on it just about a year after its release. Extraction released before every other game added a PvPvE component or tried a “fresh new take” on the genre, when “extraction shooter” was almost another way to say “ Escape from Tarkov .” Ubisoft was treading on barely charted waters at the time, muddling through loosely defined tenets of an arcane category. The result was like a medieval painter drawing a tiger without ever seeing one. Instead of being an extraction shooter with heavy PvE elements, Ubisoft’s title is a PvE-focused game that slightly borrows from the extraction genre—and even that was a sizable gamble at the time. There’s no scavenging for treasure to flip, no rushing to the exit because you found a rare material needed to improve your base. The stakes just aren’t that high. Failing to escape instead marks your character as MIA and costs some XP, and getting them back requires a full-scale rescue mission. You get a few mulligans thanks to the game’s impressive 20-operator lineup, even if it means having to bring lower-level reinforcements. Admittedly, Extraction handles progression pretty well. Leveling an operator unlocks more weapons (drawn largely from their pool in Siege ) and improves their unique gadget, giving you more charges or a smaller cooldown. Team composition also plays a role in your strategy, so you’re encouraged to level a few operators just in case you need them. But that underlying structure doesn’t matter that much when layered on top of a repetitive, almost shallow gameplay loop. Though there is no full-fledged battle pass, the game is fairly generous with its cosmetics, offering them through missions, achievements, or in the in-game shop. Proteans—a special boss archaean that mimics operators—may drop unique skins for each character, and the weekly higher-difficulty missions award some premium currency. There is something to grind for, but it’s not enough to carry the game. Not every operator has an Archaean skin, but the ones who do can look even cooler.
